in respect of moral character, there are three forms, Vice, Imperfect, Self-Control, and Brutishness.
Of the two former it is plain what the contraries are, for we call the one virtue the other self-control,
and as answering to Brutishness it will be most suitable to assign superhuman, i.e. heroical
and godlike virtue, as, in Homer, Priam says of Hector, that he was very excellent, nor was
he like the offspring of mortal man, but of a god.

Next, we must take a different point to start from, and observe that of what is to be avoided
in respect of moral character.
There are three forms, vice, imperfect self-control, and brutishness.
Of the two former, it is plain what the contraries are, for we call the one virtue, the other
self-control.
And as answering to brutishness, it will be most suitable to assign superhuman, i.e.,
heroical and godlike virtue.
As, in Homer, Priam says of Hector, that he was very excellent, nor was he like the offspring
of mortal man, but of a god.
And so, if, as is commonly said, men are raised to the position of gods by reason of very high
excellence in virtue, the state opposed to the brutish will plainly be of this nature.
Because as brutes are not virtuous or vicious, so neither are gods.
But the state of these is something more precious than virtue, of the former something
different in kind from vice.
